newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis urged to fight U.S., resist no-fly zones.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis urged to fight U.S., resist no-fly zones.

text.p: Iraqis were urged on Saturday to declare holy war on the United States while a government newspaper said Washington's control over Kurdish northern Iraq had collapsed.

"We have no alternative...but to declare Jihad (holy war) and fight them (Americans) until the last drop in Iraqis' veins...and strongly reject all their means and commandments," declared Babel, the newspaper of President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, in a front-page editorial.
"We denounce all their latitudes and longitudes. Death is better for us all if our country's territory, waters and people are not united," Babel said.
The Pentagon said on Friday that 44 cruise missile strikes against southern Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday severely damaged Iraqi air defences, destroying or damaging up to 11 of 15 targets.

In retaliation for Iraq's military assault in northern Kurdish areas, the United States also expanded the southern no-fly zone from the 32nd parallel to the 33rd, bringing it close to the outskirts of Baghdad.
Babel said Washington's missiles would not force Baghdad into submission and lambasted Clinton and his administration for "turning the White House into a dark cave inhabited by black pirates."
"True their bombs and missiles can kill and destroy but they will never, ever be able to kill our will and adherence to our country's sovereignty and national dignity," said Babel.
Saddam has said Baghdad would no longer recognise the U.S.-led no-fly zones over southern and northern Iraq.
Iraq said U.S. and allied warplanes flew 80 sorties over its territory on Friday but its air defences were unable to shoot down any of them.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya ridiculed U.S. claims that its missile raids had helped redress the situation in northern Iraq and the main Kurdish city of Arbil, which the Iraqis captured for a pro-Baghdad Kurdish faction last Saturday.

"They will never be able to change the new political and military balance in Iraqi Kurdistan. Iraq once again proves that it is the decisive force in Iraqi Kurdistan...the liberation of Arbil marks (the beginning) of the great collapse in U.S. plans against it."

The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which was ousted from Arbil last week, said on Friday the rival Iraqi-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) had attacked positions in five villages around Halabja, 10 km (six miles) from the Iranian border.
The PUK said KDP and Iraqi forces had started to advance from Arbil along the north route towards the PUK stronghold of Sulaimaniya via Degala and the key town of Koi Sanjaq.

But U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Friday Washington was satisfied Iraqi troops were leaving Kurdish areas after their offensive into the safe haven set up for Kurds in northern Iraq by the U.S.-led alliance after the 1991 Gulf war.
Asked by reporters in Washington if he was satisfied with the withdrawal of Iraqi forces from northern Iraq, Perry said: "So far, so good."
